advances.name: Keshig Tradition
advances.text: The keshig, the imperial bodyguard established by Genghis Khan himself, served as both personal guard and training school for the Mongol elite. Drawn from the sons of loyal vassals, keshig warriors received the finest equipment and training.

advances.name: Imperial Relay Network
advances.text: The yam postal relay system that once connected the vast Mongol Empire continues to function, carrying messages and officials across the steppe with remarkable speed.

advances.name: Dual Administration
advances.text: The Yuan combined Mongol tribal governance with Chinese bureaucratic administration, creating a hybrid system where the Privy Council managed military affairs while the Central Secretariat handled civil matters.

advances.name: Great Yuan Mandate
advances.text: The claim to the dynastic name of the Great Yuan, Da Yuan, carries the weight of Kublai Khan's legacy and the mandate to rule all under heaven.

advances.name: Border Provisioning
advances.text: Granaries and supply depots along the steppe-agrarian frontier ensure that nomadic populations can weather harsh winters and sustain military campaigns.

advances.name: Genghisid Legitimacy
advances.text: Among the Mongols, only descendants of Genghis Khan through his son Jochi, Chagatai, Ogedei, or Tolui may hold the title of khan. This Genghisid principle is the bedrock of Northern Yuan political legitimacy.

advances.name: Tammachi Garrisons
advances.text: The tammachi were garrison forces stationed in conquered territories, a blend of Mongol military discipline and local recruitment that provided permanent defensive capability.

advances.name: Silk Road Tribute
advances.text: Control over sections of the ancient Silk Road trade routes allows the Northern Yuan to extract tribute from passing caravans, sustaining the treasury even as territorial holdings shrink.

advances.name: Khubilai's Bureaucracy
advances.text: The administrative machinery established by Kublai Khan, adapted from Chinese models, persists in the Yuan governing tradition, census-taking, tax collection, and provincial administration by appointed officials.

advances.name: Chao Currency System
advances.text: The Yuan dynasty pioneered the use of paper currency, the chao, backed by imperial decree rather than precious metal. This innovation, radical for its time, facilitated trade across the vast Mongol domains.

advances.name: Composite Bow Workshops
advances.text: The Mongol composite bow, crafted from layers of horn, sinew, and wood, remains the deadliest ranged weapon of the steppe. Specialized workshops ensure a steady supply of these weapons.

advances.name: Imperial Court Culture
advances.text: The Yuan court blended Mongol, Chinese, Tibetan, and Persian cultural traditions into a cosmopolitan synthesis unmatched in the medieval world.

advances.name: Yuan Heavy Cavalry
advances.text: Building on both Mongol horsemanship and Chinese cataphract traditions, the Yuan heavy cavalry combines the mobility of steppe warfare with the shock power of armored lancers.

advances.name: Steppe Retreat Tactics
advances.text: After losing China, the Northern Yuan perfected the art of strategic withdrawal into the vast steppe, using the endless grasslands as both shield and sanctuary.

advances.name: Dayan Khan's Revival
advances.text: Batumongke Dayan Khan's reunification of the Mongol tribes in the late fifteenth century restored centralized authority and military effectiveness to the fragmented steppe confederation.

event.title: The Restoration of the Six Tumen
event.text:
In the late fifteenth century, a young prince of the Borjigin lineage emerged from obscurity to reunite the fractured Mongol tribes. Taking the name Dayan Khan, 'Khan of the Great Yuan', Batumongke subdued rival clans and reorganized the eastern Mongol tribes into six tumen, each a division of ten thousand warriors divided between left and right wings. With the warrior queen Mandukhai Khatun fighting at his side, Dayan Khan crushed the Oirat confederacy and restored a measure of unity not seen since the fall of Dadu.

The question now is how this restored order should be governed. Centralized command under the Great Khan's direct authority would forge a disciplined military machine, but the steppe has always been governed by consensus among equals, and the Borjigin princes expect autonomy over their own tumen.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: The Six Tumen shall answer to one Khan alone.

modifiers.name: Order of the Six Tumen
modifiers.text: Dayan Khan's reorganization of the eastern Mongol tribes into six tumen divisions has restored centralized military command across the steppe. Each tumen answers to a Borjigin prince, but all answer to the Great Khan.

options.text: Let each prince govern his own domain in the Borjigin way.

modifiers.name: Borjigin Autonomy
modifiers.text: Rather than impose rigid centralization, the Great Khan has granted his Borjigin kinsmen wide latitude to govern their own domains. This confederation of princes, bound by blood and loyalty rather than bureaucratic hierarchy, preserves the steppe tradition of consensual rule.

advances.name: Six Tumen Reform
advances.text: The reorganization of the eastern Mongol tribes into six tumen (the Three Left Wing (Chakhar, Khalkha, Uriyangkhan) and Three Right Wing (Ordos, Tumed, Yongshebu)) restored the decimal military system of Genghis Khan.

advances.name: Horse-Tea Trade
advances.text: The formalized exchange of Mongol horses for Chinese tea became the economic lifeline of the Northern Yuan, replacing raiding with regular commerce at designated border markets.

event.title: The Horse-Tea Trade
event.text:
After decades of raids and reprisals, an accommodation has been reached between the steppe and the settled world. Border markets have opened where Mongol horses, furs, and hides are exchanged for Chinese tea, silk, and grain. The Ming call it 'tribute trade' to preserve face; the Mongols call it what it is, commerce between equals.

The horse-tea trade transforms the economy of the steppe. Where once the only way to acquire Chinese goods was through plunder, now Mongol herders can trade their surplus livestock for the commodities that make steppe life bearable. Tea in particular has become a staple, without it, the monotonous diet of meat and dairy is nearly unendurable.

options.text: Trade enriches both the steppe and the farmland.

advances.name: Mongol Script Revival
advances.text: The revival and standardization of the traditional Mongolian vertical script preserves the literary heritage of the steppe peoples, from the Secret History of the Mongols to Buddhist sutras.

advances.name: Gelugpa Conversion
advances.text: The adoption of Tibetan Buddhism's Gelugpa (Yellow Hat) school as the dominant religion of the Mongols, catalyzed by Altan Khan's historic meeting with the Third Dalai Lama in 1578.

event.title: The Meeting at Chabchiyal
event.text:
In 1578, Altan Khan of the Tumed Mongols invited the Third Dalai Lama, Sonam Gyatso, to a historic meeting at Chabchiyal. The encounter transformed both parties: Altan Khan bestowed the title 'Dalai Lama' upon Sonam Gyatso, who in turn recognized the Mongol ruler as a reincarnation of Kublai Khan. This exchange of legitimacy (temporal power sanctifying spiritual authority, spiritual authority sanctifying temporal power) set in motion the mass conversion of the Mongols to Tibetan Buddhism.

Monasteries began to appear across the steppe, monks replaced shamans as spiritual advisors to the nobility, and the violent customs of traditional nomadic life softened under Buddhist influence. Yet not all welcomed this transformation. The old Tengrist traditions ran deep in the blood of the steppe warriors, and some saw the new religion as a foreign imposition that would drain the martial spirit of the Mongol nation.

options.text: The Dharma shall illuminate the steppe.

modifiers.name: Dharma Raja of the Steppe
modifiers.text: The adoption of Tibetan Buddhism as the state religion has transformed the spiritual landscape of the Mongol world. Monasteries rise across the steppe, and the bond between lama and khan legitimizes rule through both spiritual and temporal authority.

options.text: The Eternal Blue Sky needs no replacement.

modifiers.name: Tengrism Endures
modifiers.text: The old ways of the Eternal Blue Sky have not been abandoned. While foreign religions have their place, the Mongol warrior tradition draws its strength from the reverence of Tengri, the open sky, and the spirits of the ancestors.

advances.name: Khorchin Alliance
advances.text: The Khorchin Mongols, dwelling on the eastern plains, served as crucial military allies, their light cavalry scouts providing intelligence and screening forces for the main army.

advances.name: Steppe Law Code
advances.text: Building on the Yasa of Genghis Khan, later Northern Yuan rulers codified steppe customary law into formal legal codes governing property, marriage, and criminal justice.

advances.name: Altan Khan's Diplomacy
advances.text: Altan Khan's diplomatic opening with the Ming dynasty in 1571 ended decades of border warfare and established regular trade relations, proving that the pen could achieve what the sword could not. On the Tumed plain his Chinese settlers raised the baishin, walled farming towns, and the city of Hohhot grew from them.

advances.name: Dharma Patronage
advances.text: Royal patronage of Buddhist monasteries and scholars created centers of learning across the steppe, where monks translated scriptures, practiced medicine, and preserved astronomical knowledge.

advances.name: Tumen Commanders
advances.text: The tradition of appointing proven warriors as tumen commanders, leaders of ten thousand, ensured that military command remained tied to demonstrated competence on the battlefield.

advances.name: Chakhar Baaturs
advances.text: The baaturs, champion warriors, of the Chakhar formed the personal guard of Ligdan Khan, the last Great Khan of the Mongols. Three hundred strong, they were the finest horsemen and fighters of the steppe.

event.title: The Defiance of Ligdan Khan
event.text:
Ligdan Khan, the last to bear the title of Great Khan of the Mongols, has raised his Chakhar warriors in desperate defiance against the rising Manchu power. With his corps of three hundred baaturs, elite warriors sworn to personal loyalty, Ligdan has attempted to centralize authority over the fractious Mongol tumen, even as one tribe after another defects to the banner of Hong Taiji.

The contest is unequal: the Manchu combine Mongol cavalry traditions with Chinese administrative efficiency, while Ligdan's harsh centralization drives his own allies into enemy arms. Yet his defiance represents the last assertion of independent Mongol sovereignty, a refusal to accept that the legacy of Genghis Khan has passed to foreign hands.

options.text: The blood of Genghis Khan does not bend the knee.

advances.name: Ligdan's Centralization
advances.text: Ligdan Khan's attempt to restore direct imperial authority over all Mongol tribes through appointed officials and centralized taxation, a bold but ultimately divisive reform.

advances.name: Last Khan's Defiance
advances.text: Even as the Manchu threat grows and allies defect, the fighting spirit of the last Mongol khans refuses to yield. Every battle lost only strengthens the resolve to resist.

advances.name: Nomadic Adaptation
advances.text: The centuries of Northern Yuan existence proved that nomadic economies could adapt and thrive, incorporating trade goods and agricultural products into the traditional pastoral cycle.

advances.name: Preservation of the Great Seal
advances.text: The jade seal of the Great Yuan dynasty, a physical symbol of the imperial mandate, was preserved by successive khans as proof that the legitimate dynasty endured on the steppe.

advances.name: Steppe Modernization
advances.text: Contact with neighboring civilizations and internal pressures drive reforms in manufacturing and production, adapting settled technologies to the needs of the steppe economy.

advances.name: Chinggisid Renaissance
advances.text: A cultural revival celebrating the heritage of Genghis Khan and the Great Mongol Empire (in literature, law, and the arts) as the foundation of a distinct Mongol national identity.

advances.name: Eternal Mandate
advances.text: The Great Yuan mandate, transmitted through the Borjigin bloodline from Genghis Khan to the present day, is not merely a political claim but a cosmic truth, the Eternal Blue Sky chose this lineage to rule.

advances.name: Cavalry Reformation
advances.text: The ancient cavalry traditions of the steppe are reformed for the modern era, integrating new tactics and training methods while preserving the core Mongol advantages of mobility and archery.

advances.name: Great Yuan Legacy
advances.text: The legacy of the Great Yuan, an empire that once stretched from Korea to Hungary, endures as an inspiration and aspiration for the Mongol nation.

units.name: Keshig Guard
units.text: The elite imperial bodyguard of the Great Khan, the keshig are drawn from the sons of loyal Borjigin nobles and trained in both mounted archery and heavy cavalry combat. Their loyalty is absolute.

units.name: Yuan Lancer
units.text: Armored heavy cavalry combining Mongol horsemanship with Chinese cataphract traditions. These lancers carry both lance and composite bow, capable of devastating charges followed by mounted archery.

units.name: Chakhar Baatur
units.text: The baaturs, champion warriors, of the Chakhar tribe, serving as the personal guard of the last Great Khan. Ferocious in attack and unshakeable in defense, they embody the last flame of Mongol independence.

units.name: Tammachi
units.text: Garrison troops drawn from settled Mongol-Chinese border populations. The tammachi combine infantry discipline with knowledge of local terrain, defending the frontier between steppe and farmland.

units.name: Khorchin Scout
units.text: Light cavalry from the eastern Khorchin Mongols, masters of scouting, raiding, and the feigned retreat. They ride the fleetest horses and strike where the enemy least expects.

units.name: Tumen Horse
units.text: The herdsmen of the six tumen, called out by wing and banner with their own bows and their own strings of ponies.

units.name: Chakhar Carbineers
units.text: Chakhar horsemen who carry a carbine beside the saddle bow, drilled to fire from the saddle and ride on.

buildings.name: Imperial Yam Station
buildings.text: A relay post in the yam system, the Mongol Empire's network of staging points that enabled messages and officials to cross the steppe at extraordinary speed.

buildings.name: Yuan Secretariat
buildings.text: An administrative bureau adapted from the Chinese Zhongshu Sheng, staffed by literate officials who manage civil affairs, taxation, and census records in the Yuan tradition.

buildings.name: Steppe Granary
buildings.text: Food storage facilities on the steppe-agrarian frontier, ensuring that nomadic populations and garrison forces can survive harsh winters and sustain military operations.

buildings.name: Tibetan Buddhist Temple
buildings.text: A monastery of the Gelugpa school, where Tibetan monks teach the Dharma to Mongol converts. These temples serve as centers of literacy, medicine, and cultural exchange.

buildings.name: Border Trading Post
buildings.text: A designated market on the steppe-agrarian frontier where Mongol horses, furs, and hides are exchanged for Chinese tea, silk, and grain.

buildings.name: Eight White Yurts
buildings.text: The tent shrine of Chinggis Khan, kept by the Darkhad who are freed of every other duty. Before these yurts a khan of the Great Yuan is raised on the white felt.

buildings.name: Composite Bow Workshop
buildings.text: A bowyers' workshop where horn, sinew and wood are glued in layers and left to cure for a year, the work behind every bow of the steppe.

buildings.name: Pingzhun Treasury
buildings.text: An exchange treasury of the paper currency, where chao is changed for silver at the official rate and worn notes are redeemed for new.

buildings.name: Darughachi Office
buildings.text: The seat of a darughachi, the resident overseer who holds the seal of a town, counts its households and gathers its tax for the khan.

buildings.name: Baishin
buildings.text: A walled settlement of Chinese farmers and craftsmen on the pasture, tilling millet and wheat for a nomad lord in return for his protection.

buildings.name: Mamba Datsan
buildings.text: The medical college of a monastery, where lamas study the Four Tantras, gather herbs and compound remedies for herders and princes alike.

list.name: Branch Secretariats
list.text: The Central Secretariat ruled the country around the capital. Everything else went to its branches, the Xing Zhongshu Sheng: in the end eleven copies of the central office, each sent out to govern a conquered land under chancellors who were almost always Mongols or Semuren, never Han. They began as headquarters that moved with the armies and stayed where the armies stopped. Later dynasties renamed and redrew them, and the provinces of China descend from them.

list.name: Shumi Yuan
list.text: The Bureau of Military Affairs (Shumi Yuan), rebuilt by Khubilai Khan in 1263, was an exclusively Mongol-Semuren preserve. Where the Zhongshu Sheng admitted Han participation in civil affairs, the Shumi Yuan commanded the keshig units, the tammachi border garrisons, and the imperial tumen with no Han-ren in senior rank for the dynasty's first century. By 1287 it answered only to the khan, coequal of the civil secretariat. The institution expressed a structural Yuan principle: arms remain in the hands of the conquering people.

list.name: Branch Censorates
list.text: Khubilai Khan's decree of 1268 raised the Censorate to equal rank with the civil and military secretariats. What no earlier dynasty had was its branches: a Branch Censorate for Jiangnan and another for Shaanxi, each sending inspectors on circuit through the provinces beneath it, with the right to impeach a branch chancellor. The khans valued them as a check on their own governors. The inspectors collided endlessly with the Mongol nobility, whose ortoq trading partnerships they investigated.

list.name: Semu Caste Hierarchy
list.text: The defining political innovation of Yuan rule was the formal four-tier ethnic classification: Mongols, then Semuren ('various-eyed people': Persians, Tanguts, Tibetans, Uighurs, Turks, Europeans), then Han-ren of the former Jin, then Nan-ren of the former Southern Song. The tiers determined access to senior office, judicial standing, weapon privileges, and tax assessment. The system gave the throne a vast pool of foreign-born loyalists who owed everything to the dynasty, and seeded the Han-ren rebellions that ended Yuan rule.

list.name: Phags-pa Script Apparatus
list.text: In 1269 Khubilai Khan commissioned the young Tibetan lama Drogon Chogyal Phagpa to create a single phonetic script that could transcribe every language of the empire (Mongolian, Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit, Uighur, Persian) in one unified set of squared letters. Imperial decree made it the official script of the dynasty: state seals, coinage, and the parallel-text edicts of the Bureau of National Languages all bore Phags-pa lettering. The Bureau also served as the institutional scaffold for Phagpa's role as Imperial Preceptor (Dishi), linking the Yuan throne to the Sa-skya monastery of Tibet.

list.name: Yan Zheng
list.text: Yuan fiscal policy depended on the salt monopoly (yan zheng) administered from Yangzhou. Pressed to extreme heights by the ministers Lu Shi-rong (executed 1285) and Sangha (executed 1291), the Yan Yun Si commission monopolised production at the coastal salterns of Liang-zhe and Liang-huai, distributed product through licensed merchants paid in yan-yin certificate-warrants, and remitted revenue directly to the Imperial Treasury. Salt accounted for as much as eighty per cent of central government income at peak. The dependency was the dynasty's strength and weakness: when the Yangzi rebellions of the 1350s disrupted southern salt extraction, central revenue collapsed within a decade.
